bibl.title: Half-Life of Serum Elimination of Perfluorooctanesulfonate,Perfluorohexanesulfonate, and Perfluorooctanoate in Retired Fluorochemical Production Worke

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: the rate at which three perfluoroalkyl acids leave human serum, measured in people whose exposure has stopped
span.quote: The purpose of this observational study was to estimate the elimination half-life of PFOS, PFHS, and PFOA from human serum.

span.label: how long PFOS, PFHS and PFOA persist in human serum once occupational exposure ends, a number previously available only by extrapolation from monkeys and rodents
span.quote: The purpose of this observational study was to estimate the elimination half-life of PFOS, PFHS, and PFOA from human serum.

span.label: the first direct human serum elimination half-lives for PFOS, PFHS and PFOA, from 26 retired fluorochemical workers followed for five years
span.quote: Twenty-six (24 male, 2 female) retired fluorochemical production workers, with no additional occupational exposure, had periodic blood samples collected over 5 years, with serum stored in plastic vials at −80°C.

span.label: existence
span.quote: Based on these data, humans appear to have a long half-life of serum elimination of PFOS, PFHS, and PFOA. Differences in species-specific pharmacokinetics may be due, in part, to a saturable renal resorption process.

span.label: serum elimination of perfluoroalkyl acids that is slow enough in humans, and fast enough in every other species measured, that the interspecies gap is itself the finding
span.quote: Nevertheless, the present study data strongly indicate that humans are very slow eliminators of these three perfluoroalkyl acids compared with other species.

span.label: observational cohort with repeated venous sampling over five years, HPLC-mass spectrometry against labelled internal standards, and a first-order elimination model fitted per subject
span.term: observational cohort with repeated venous sampling over five years, HPLC-mass spectrometry against labelled internal standards, and a first-order elimination model fitted per subject
span.quote: We used WinNonlin software, version 4.1 (Pharsight Corporation, Mountain View, CA) to calculate the half-life of elimination based on the mean value of the split analyses. The data were linear when plotted as the logarithm of serum concentration versus time. Therefore, we assumed a first order model.

span.label: a high-affinity transporter returns filtered perfluoroalkyl acid from the renal tubule to the blood; because it saturates, the elimination rate depends on concentration and on how much transporter a species expresses
span.quote: Based on these data, humans appear to have a long half-life of serum elimination of PFOS, PFHS, and PFOA. Differences in species-specific pharmacokinetics may be due, in part, to a saturable renal resorption process.

span.label: species and sexes differ in which proximal-tubule anion transporters they express, so the same molecule is returned to the blood at different rates - offered as the reason the human half-life is years and the rat's is days
span.term: differential expression of organic anion transporters
span.quote: The diversity of proximal tubular organic anion transporters and potential for genetic variation have indicated that the long elimination half-life in humans compared with that in other species may be due to differential expression of organic anion transporters and could be linked to either low-level transport into urine or increased tubular resorption.

span.label: the C-F bond's stability and the high electronegativity of perfluorinated alkyl acids make metabolism unfavourable, so elimination is the only route of loss and half-life is set entirely by excretion
span.term: metabolic stability of the carbon-fluorine bond
span.quote: Because of the stability of the carbon–fluorine bond and the high electronegativity of perfluorinated alkyl acids, metabolism would not be favored; thus, perfluorohexanesulfonate (PFHS) is also not expected to be metabolized.

span.label: the authors state that human pharmacokinetics is not likely to be one-compartment, in the same discussion that reports half-lives fitted with a one-compartment first-order model - the model is disclaimed and its output is the paper's headline number
span.quote: The actual pharmacokinetics of PFOS, PFHS, and PFOA in humans is not likely to be consistent with a one-compartment distribution in spite of the present data fit to a first order model.

span.label: continuing non-occupational exposure could flatten the observed decline, so the half-lives may be biased long; the paper raises this and does not quantify it
span.quote: It is possible that the rate of elimination may have resulted in more shallow slopes as concentrations declined because of the influence of environmental exposure.

span.label: the model was selected by looking at a semi-log plot, not by comparing candidate models - linearity by eye is the entire justification for first-order kinetics
span.quote: For each of the 26 subjects, the elimination appeared linear on a semi-log plot of concentration versus time; therefore, we used a first-order model for estimation.

span.label: 26 subjects, 24 of them male, all retired from two plants of one company; the two women are the whole basis for the sex comparison
span.quote: The two female subjects (subjects 7 and 25) had arithmetic mean serum elimination half-lives similar to those calculated for males, respectively, for PFOS (5.9 years vs. 5.4 years; p = 0.87) and PFOA (3.3 years vs. 3.8 years; p = 0.69), and non-significantly higher for PFHS (12.8 years vs. 8.2 years; p = 0.23).

span.label: three of the original participants had post-baseline occupational exposure: one was dropped entirely, one truncated, one's start point moved for a single analyte - principled and disclosed, but the cohort is not the cohort recruited
span.quote: During the review of the subjects’ questionnaire data, we determined that three Decatur retirees likely had additional occupational exposure after their initial blood collection in November 1998. One retiree had intermittently worked with fluorochemicals at the Decatur facility throughout the study period. This retiree was excluded from the entire data analysis. A second Decatur retiree had intermittently worked in the Decatur facility until February 2001; therefore, his data were truncated until that point in time. A third Decatur retiree likely had occupational exposure to PFOA between his initial (November 1998) and second (June 1999) blood collections that affected his assessment; therefore, we used June 1999 as his initial time point for measurement of PFOA.

span.label: first-order elimination kinetics and the half-life construct, carried from single-dose animal pharmacokinetics onto an observational human cohort with no known dose and no defined time zero
span.quote: We used WinNonlin software, version 4.1 (Pharsight Corporation, Mountain View, CA) to calculate the half-life of elimination based on the mean value of the split analyses. The data were linear when plotted as the logarithm of serum concentration versus time. Therefore, we assumed a first order model.

span.label: the renal transporter explanation, carried from rodent sex-difference studies to account for a between-species difference in humans
span.quote: The diversity of proximal tubular organic anion transporters and potential for genetic variation have indicated that the long elimination half-life in humans compared with that in other species may be due to differential expression of organic anion transporters and could be linked to either low-level transport into urine or increased tubular resorption.

span.label: split analyses of the same blood collection, to separate assay variability from real decline
span.note: eliminates: assay variability being read as a fall in serum concentration, since both halves of the split come from one blood collection · outcome: held
span.quote: A total of 189 (96%) of the 197 blood collections had sufficient sample available for split analyses. Spearman Rho correlations exceeded 0.98 for each analyte.

span.label: spiked recovery and precision at three PFOA concentrations spanning the assay range
span.note: eliminates: a half-life derived from an assay that is accurate at one concentration and not across the decline it is measuring · outcome: held
span.quote: For PFOA, we used three spiked samples with targeted means of 80, 240, and 750 ng/mL. Recovered means ranged between 93.3 and 101.5%. Coefficients of variation (CVs) ranged between 1.4 and 3.8.

span.label: spiked recovery and precision for PFHS, the analyte with the longest and most variable half-life
span.note: eliminates: the same, for the analyte whose half-life is longest and most variable and therefore rests on the most measurements · outcome: partial
span.quote: For PFHS, recovered means ranged between 88.6 and 105.2%, with CVs ranging between 6.9 and 11.9.

span.label: blank rabbit or calf serum run with each batch, to detect contamination in a laboratory that also handled these compounds
span.note: eliminates: contamination of the samples in a laboratory that also handled these compounds - a blank that comes back clean on each run is what separates measured serum from carry-over
span.quote: Blank rabbit or calf serum was evaluated with each run, and the spiked matrix was used for matrix-matched standard curve extractions.

span.label: end-of-study concentrations checked against general-population reference values, to show the decline was not floored by background exposure
span.note: eliminates: an elimination rate flattened by continuing background exposure, which would lengthen every half-life in the study · outcome: held
span.quote: It is unlikely that the potential for non-occupational exposures substantially distorted the elimination rates calculated as median end-of-study concentrations for PFOS (295 ng/mL), PFHS (117 ng/mL), and PFOA (148 ng/mL), which remained above comparable estimates of 30.4, 2.1, and 5.2 ng/mL, respectively, reported for a statistically representative sample of the U.S. general population.

span.label: the same check applied per subject rather than to the median, which is where it stops holding for four of the 26
span.note: eliminates: a median that holds while individuals do not - the per-subject form is where the check stops holding, for four of twenty-six · outcome: partial
span.quote: Furthermore, only four study subjects (subjects 1–4) had end-of-study PFOS concentrations that were below the upper 95% CI of the geometric mean of the 95th percentile as reported by Calafat et al. (97.5 ng/mL).

span.label: regression of half-life on age, years worked, job and time since retirement, to test whether the estimate tracks anything about the person rather than the chemistry
span.note: eliminates: a half-life that tracks age, tenure, job or time since retirement rather than the chemistry of the compound · outcome: held
span.quote: We used multiple regression to determine statistically significant (p < 0.05) associations between the half-life of elimination for PFOS, PFHS, and PFOA and explanatory variables including initial and end-of-study perfluorochemical concentration, age at study onset, years worked, and years since retirement.

span.label: self-reported disease and medication review, for renal or hepatic conditions that would alter clearance
span.note: eliminates: altered renal or hepatic clearance in a subject being reported as the elimination rate of the compound · outcome: held
span.quote: A review of each subject’s self-reported diseases and medications did not provide additional evidence of possible associations with the half-lives of serum elimination. No renal diseases were reported by the 26 subjects.

span.label: half-life of serum elimination
span.quote: Based on these data, humans appear to have a long half-life of serum elimination of PFOS, PFHS, and PFOA. Differences in species-specific pharmacokinetics may be due, in part, to a saturable renal resorption process.

span.label: first-order model
span.quote: For each of the 26 subjects, the elimination appeared linear on a semi-log plot of concentration versus time; therefore, we used a first-order model for estimation.

span.label: semi-log plot
span.quote: For each of the 26 subjects, the elimination appeared linear on a semi-log plot of concentration versus time; therefore, we used a first-order model for estimation.

span.label: PFOS
span.quote: The purpose of this observational study was to estimate the elimination half-life of PFOS, PFHS, and PFOA from human serum.

span.label: PFHS
span.quote: The purpose of this observational study was to estimate the elimination half-life of PFOS, PFHS, and PFOA from human serum.

span.label: PFOA
span.quote: The purpose of this observational study was to estimate the elimination half-life of PFOS, PFHS, and PFOA from human serum.

span.label: retired fluorochemical production workers
span.quote: Twenty-six (24 male, 2 female) retired fluorochemical production workers, with no additional occupational exposure, had periodic blood samples collected over 5 years, with serum stored in plastic vials at −80°C.

span.label: saturable renal resorption
span.quote: Based on these data, humans appear to have a long half-life of serum elimination of PFOS, PFHS, and PFOA. Differences in species-specific pharmacokinetics may be due, in part, to a saturable renal resorption process.

span.label: organic anion transporters
span.quote: The diversity of proximal tubular organic anion transporters and potential for genetic variation have indicated that the long elimination half-life in humans compared with that in other species may be due to differential expression of organic anion transporters and could be linked to either low-level transport into urine or increased tubular resorption.

span.label: tubular resorption
span.quote: The diversity of proximal tubular organic anion transporters and potential for genetic variation have indicated that the long elimination half-life in humans compared with that in other species may be due to differential expression of organic anion transporters and could be linked to either low-level transport into urine or increased tubular resorption.

span.label: internal standard
span.quote: At the end of the study, we used HPLC-mass spectrometry to analyze the samples, with quantification based on the ion ratios for PFOS and PFHS and the internal standard 18O2-PFOS. For PFOA, quantitation was based on the internal standard 13C2-PFOA.

span.label: lower limit of quantitation
span.quote: The lower limit of quantitation (LOQ) was set as the lowest acceptable standard value fitted on the standard curves used. For all analyses, regardless of instrumentation used, the lower limit of quantitation was 10.0 ng/mL.

span.label: split analyses
span.quote: A total of 189 (96%) of the 197 blood collections had sufficient sample available for split analyses. Spearman Rho correlations exceeded 0.98 for each analyte.

span.label: linear isomer
span.quote: The PFOA standard contained the linear isomer at 78% and the combined branched chain isomers at 22%.

span.label: branched chain isomers
span.quote: The PFOA standard contained the linear isomer at 78% and the combined branched chain isomers at 22%.

span.label: cynomolgus monkeys
span.quote: The serum elimination half-life of PFOA in the present study’s 26 retired fluorochemical production workers is considerably longer than the elimination half-life in cynomolgus monkeys (approximately 14–40 days) after either repeated daily oral doses or a single intravenous injection.

span.label: ion ratios
span.quote: At the end of the study, we used HPLC-mass spectrometry to analyze the samples, with quantification based on the ion ratios for PFOS and PFHS and the internal standard 18O2-PFOS. For PFOA, quantitation was based on the internal standard 13C2-PFOA.

span.label: environmental exposure
span.quote: It is possible that the rate of elimination may have resulted in more shallow slopes as concentrations declined because of the influence of environmental exposure.

span.label: rate of elimination
span.quote: It is possible that the rate of elimination may have resulted in more shallow slopes as concentrations declined because of the influence of environmental exposure.

span.label: right skewness
span.quote: Median values and ranges are also reported in Table 3 and indicate the right skewness of the distribution, as visualized in Figure 2.

span.label: half-life of serum elimination - the ARITHMETIC mean over the 26 subjects: 5.4 y for PFOS, 8.5 y for PFHS, 3.8 y for PFOA
span.quote: The arithmetic and geometric mean half-lives of serum elimination, respectively, were 5.4 years [95% confidence interval (CI), 3.9–6.9] and 4.8 years (95% CI, 4.0–5.8) for PFOS; 8.5 years (95% CI, 6.4–10.6) and 7.3 years (95% CI, 5.8–9.2) for PFHS; and 3.8 years (95% CI, 3.1–4.4) and 3.5 years (95% CI, 3.0–4.1) for PFOA.

span.label: half-life of serum elimination - the GEOMETRIC mean over the same 26 subjects: 4.8 y for PFOS, 7.3 y for PFHS, 3.5 y for PFOA. These are the three numbers later papers quote as the half-life, without naming the statistic
span.quote: The arithmetic and geometric mean half-lives of serum elimination, respectively, were 5.4 years [95% confidence interval (CI), 3.9–6.9] and 4.8 years (95% CI, 4.0–5.8) for PFOS; 8.5 years (95% CI, 6.4–10.6) and 7.3 years (95% CI, 5.8–9.2) for PFHS; and 3.8 years (95% CI, 3.1–4.4) and 3.5 years (95% CI, 3.0–4.1) for PFOA.

span.label: half-life of serum elimination - the arithmetic mean after removing the two longest-eliminating subjects, which collapses onto the geometric mean and shows the gap between the first two senses is two people
span.quote: Excluding subjects 19 and 24, the two subjects with the highest half-lives of serum elimination for PFOS and PFHS that appear in Figure 2, the arithmetic mean half-lives of elimination for PFOS and PFHS reduced to 4.8 years (95% CI, 4.1–5.4) and 7.8 years (95% CI, 6.3–9.3), respectively. These arithmetic mean values were then similar to the geometric mean and median values reported in Table 3 when each of these subjects was included in the analyses.

span.label: builds-on → Calafat et al.'s NHANES estimates of general-population serum concentrations, used here as the background floor the retirees had to stay above
span.quote: Furthermore, only four study subjects (subjects 1–4) had end-of-study PFOS concentrations that were below the upper 95% CI of the geometric mean of the 95th percentile as reported by Calafat et al. (97.5 ng/mL).

span.label: extends → intravenous and repeated-oral-dose pharmacokinetic studies in cynomolgus monkeys, from which human persistence had previously been extrapolated
span.quote: The serum elimination half-life of PFOA in the present study’s 26 retired fluorochemical production workers is considerably longer than the elimination half-life in cynomolgus monkeys (approximately 14–40 days) after either repeated daily oral doses or a single intravenous injection.

span.label: qualifies → one-compartment first-order pharmacokinetic modelling of perfluoroalkyl acids in humans
span.quote: The actual pharmacokinetics of PFOS, PFHS, and PFOA in humans is not likely to be consistent with a one-compartment distribution in spite of the present data fit to a first order model.

span.label: PFHS —contrasted-with→ PFOS
span.note: differs in: human serum elimination half-life and its dispersion · the relation itself is separately evidenced · strength of the relation: 0.9
span.quote: Less is known about the elimination kinetics of PFHS in other species. The results indicate the human half-life of serum elimination may be longer and more variable than that of PFOS.

span.label: retired fluorochemical production workers —contrasted-with→ cynomolgus monkeys
span.note: differs in: serum elimination half-life of PFOA · the relation itself is separately evidenced · strength of the relation: 0.9
span.quote: The serum elimination half-life of PFOA in the present study’s 26 retired fluorochemical production workers is considerably longer than the elimination half-life in cynomolgus monkeys (approximately 14–40 days) after either repeated daily oral doses or a single intravenous injection.

span.label: PFOS —operationalised-as→ ion ratios
span.note: the relation itself is separately evidenced · strength of the relation: 0.9

span.label: environmental exposure —causes→ rate of elimination
span.note: direction on the measure: reduces · the relation itself is separately evidenced · strength of the relation: 0.45 — the record marks this weak
span.quote: It is possible that the rate of elimination may have resulted in more shallow slopes as concentrations declined because of the influence of environmental exposure.

span.label: humans eliminate PFOS, PFHS and PFOA on a scale of years, every other species measured on a scale of days
span.term: humans eliminate PFOS, PFHS and PFOA on a scale of years, every other species measured on a scale of days
span.quote: The serum elimination half-life of PFOA in the present study’s 26 retired fluorochemical production workers is considerably longer than the elimination half-life in cynomolgus monkeys (approximately 14–40 days) after either repeated daily oral doses or a single intravenous injection.

span.label: the arithmetic and geometric means of the half-life differ by up to 14%, and removing two subjects collapses the difference
span.term: the arithmetic and geometric means of the half-life differ by up to 14%, and removing two subjects collapses the difference
span.quote: Excluding subjects 19 and 24, the two subjects with the highest half-lives of serum elimination for PFOS and PFHS that appear in Figure 2, the arithmetic mean half-lives of elimination for PFOS and PFHS reduced to 4.8 years (95% CI, 4.1–5.4) and 7.8 years (95% CI, 6.3–9.3), respectively. These arithmetic mean values were then similar to the geometric mean and median values reported in Table 3 when each of these subjects was included in the analyses.

span.label: PFHS has both the longest and the most variable human half-life of the three
span.term: PFHS has both the longest and the most variable human half-life of the three
span.quote: Less is known about the elimination kinetics of PFHS in other species. The results indicate the human half-life of serum elimination may be longer and more variable than that of PFOS.

span.label: no subject characteristic - age, years worked, job, time since retirement - predicts the half-life
span.term: no subject characteristic - age, years worked, job, time since retirement - predicts the half-life
span.quote: Age at study onset, time worked, usual 3M job, and time since retirement were not associated with PFOS, PFHS, or PFOA serum elimination half-lives.

span.label: the two female subjects' half-lives are statistically indistinguishable from the men's, on n=2
span.term: the two female subjects' half-lives are statistically indistinguishable from the men's, on n=2
span.quote: The two female subjects (subjects 7 and 25) had arithmetic mean serum elimination half-lives similar to those calculated for males, respectively, for PFOS (5.9 years vs. 5.4 years; p = 0.87) and PFOA (3.3 years vs. 3.8 years; p = 0.69), and non-significantly higher for PFHS (12.8 years vs. 8.2 years; p = 0.23).

span.quote: We used WinNonlin software, version 4.1 (Pharsight Corporation, Mountain View, CA) to calculate the half-life of elimination based on the mean value of the split analyses. The data were linear when plotted as the logarithm of serum concentration versus time. Therefore, we assumed a first order model.

span.label: arithmetic mean serum elimination half-life of PFHS, the longest of the three

span.quote: Their mean length of study follow-up was 1,849 days (range, 1,139–1,945 days) equivalent to a mean of 5.0 years (range, 3.1–5.3 years).
